a: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants, algae, and some bacteria convert light energy into chemical energy. It occurs in chloroplasts, which contain chlorophyll (the green pigment). The overall equation is: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. The process has two stages. The light-dependent reactions require direct sunlight and occur in the thylakoid membranes: chlorophyll absorbs light, splitting water molecules into oxygen (released), protons, and electrons, which generate ATP and NADPH. The Calvin cycle (light-independent reactions) occurs in the stroma: CO₂ is fixed into organic molecules using ATP and NADPH, producing glucose. C3 plants (most plants) use the Calvin cycle directly. C4 plants (corn, sugarcane) concentrate CO₂ to reduce photorespiration. CAM plants (cacti, succulents) open stomata at night to conserve water. Photosynthesis is the foundation of most food chains and produces the oxygen we breathe.

DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is the hereditary material in all living organisms. Its structure is a double helix — two strands wound around each other, discovered by Watson and Crick in 1953 using X-ray crystallography data from Rosalind Franklin. Each strand consists of a sugar-phosphate backbone and four nitrogen bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G), and cytosine (C). Base pairing is specific: A pairs with T (2 hydrogen bonds), G pairs with C (3 hydrogen bonds). The sequence of these bases encodes genetic information. DNA replication is semi-conservative: the double helix unwinds, and each strand serves as a template for a new complementary strand, producing two identical DNA molecules. A gene is a segment of DNA that codes for a specific protein. The human genome contains about 20,000-25,000 genes. DNA is organized into 23 pairs of chromosomes in humans. DNA profiling (fingerprinting) uses variable regions of DNA to identify individuals.

Evolution by natural selection is the central organizing principle of biology, first comprehensively described by Charles Darwin in 'On the Origin of Species' (1859). The theory proposes that all species descend from common ancestors and change over time through natural selection. Key mechanisms include: variation (individuals within a population have different traits), inheritance (traits are passed to offspring), overpopulation (more offspring are produced than can survive), and differential survival (individuals with traits better suited to the environment are more likely to survive and reproduce, passing on those traits). Over generations, this process leads to adaptation and eventually new species. Evidence for evolution includes: the fossil record (transitional forms like Tiktaalik), comparative anatomy (homologous structures like mammalian forelimbs), molecular biology (DNA similarities between species), biogeography (distribution of species), and direct observation (antibiotic resistance in bacteria, Darwin's finches). The modern synthesis combines Darwinian natural selection with Mendelian genetics.

Gravity is a fundamental force of nature that attracts objects with mass toward each other. Isaac Newton's law of universal gravitation (1687) states that every mass attracts every other mass with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them: F = G(m₁m₂)/r². Einstein's general theory of relativity (1915) revolutionized our understanding: gravity is not a force but a curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy. Massive objects like the Sun warp the fabric of spacetime, and objects like planets follow the curved paths — what we experience as gravity. General relativity predicts phenomena like gravitational time dilation (time passes slower in stronger gravity), gravitational lensing (light bends around massive objects), gravitational waves (ripples in spacetime), and black holes (regions where gravity is so strong that nothing can escape). Gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces but dominates at large scales because it is always attractive and has infinite range.

A black hole is a region of spacetime where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape. Black holes form when massive stars collapse at the end of their life cycle. Types include: stellar-mass black holes (3-20 solar masses, formed from supernova explosions), supermassive black holes (millions to billions of solar masses, found at centers of galaxies, including Sagittarius A* at our Milky Way's center), and intermediate-mass black holes. The boundary around a black hole is the event horizon — the point of no return. At the center lies the singularity, a point of infinite density where the laws of physics break down. Stephen Hawking proposed Hawking radiation (1974) — quantum effects near the event horizon cause black holes to slowly emit radiation and eventually evaporate over immense timescales. Black holes are detected through their effects on nearby matter: accretion disks (hot gas spiraling in), gravitational lensing, and gravitational waves from mergers. The first direct image of a black hole (M87*) was captured by the Event Horizon Telescope in 2019.

The periodic table organizes all known chemical elements by atomic number (number of protons). Dmitri Mendeleev created the first widely accepted version in 1869, leaving gaps for undiscovered elements whose properties he predicted. The table is arranged in rows (periods) and columns (groups/families). Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties because they have the same number of valence electrons. Key groups: alkali metals (Group 1, highly reactive), alkaline earth metals (Group 2), transition metals (Groups 3-12), halogens (Group 17, highly reactive nonmetals), and noble gases (Group 18, inert). The table also shows trends: atomic radius increases to the left and down, ionization energy increases up and to the right, and electronegativity increases up and to the right. Most elements are metals (left side), fewer are nonmetals (right side), and some are metalloids (along the staircase line, with properties of both). There are 118 confirmed elements, with 94 occurring naturally and 24 synthesized in laboratories.
